📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitalii Mykolenko played the full 90 minutes as Ukraine secured a 1-0 victory over Georgia in their latest UEFA Nations League outing.

The Everton defender made his second successive start of this international window as his nation claimed all three points, while fellow Blues Brennan Johnson and Jake O’Brien were also in action for their respective countries.

Johnson was introduced as a 63rd-minute substitute for Wales, who suffered a narrow 3-2 defeat against Portugal.

Meanwhile, O’Brien came off the bench in the second half as the Republic of Ireland recorded an impressive 3-0 victory over Kosovo, who had been reduced to 10 men before half-time.

Elsewhere, Everton youngster Braiden Graham was an unused substitute as Northern Ireland played out a 1-1 draw with Hungary.

While Wales Under-19s duo Luis Gardner and Shea Pita both played the full contest as their side overcame Iceland 3-1 on penalties.

Gardner captained the young Dragons and converted the decisive spot-kick to seal the victory.

Scotland Under-17s striker Kai Hutchison was also involved, entering the action as a second-half substitute in an entertaining 6-3 victory over Sweden.

How Claudio Ranieri’s Roma nearly scuppered Inter’s legendary treble

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “He’s right with what he remarked I am very demanding of myself and I have to win to be sure of things.
  • “Ranieri on the other hand has the mentality of someone who doesn’t need to win.
  • Industry observers note that “He is almost 70 years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “He’s right with what he remarked I am very demanding of myself and I have to win to be sure of things. This is why I have won so many trophies in my career,” was Jose Mourinho’s humble retort to Claudio Ranieri in the early months of his tenure at Inter.

“Ranieri on the other hand has the mentality of someone who doesn’t need to win.

Industry observers note that “He is almost 70 years old. He has won a Super Cup and another small trophy, and he is too old to change his mentality. He’s old and he hasn’t won anything.”.

Ranieri was in fact only 56 at the time – something that Mourinho almost certainly knew. Now – 16 years later – he is actually 73 if Mourinho feels like a more accurate rehash.

“I studied Italian five hours a day for many months to ensure I could communicate with the players, media and fans,” Mourinho added. “Ranieri had been in England for five years and still struggled to say ‘good morning’ and ‘good afternoon.'”.

While Mourinho was cementing his status as A Special One at Chelsea – doing what his predecessor couldn’t quite manage – by converting Roman Abramovich’s millions into major honours, Ranieri saw his reputation flounder with short and unsuccessful stints in charge of Valencia and Parma.

Recent findings suggest that still, the Italian was entrusted to take the reigns at newly-promoted Juventus in 2007 following Didier Deschamps’ falling out with the board. He inherited a squad boasting Gianluigi Buffon, Giorgio Chiellini, Pavel Nedved, David Trezeguet and Alessandro Del Piero as the Old Lady looked to promptly heal the scars of Calciopoli.

Ranieri led Juventus to a respectable third-place finish in their first season back, with a remit to go those couple of steps further as Mourinho – back then the sexiest name in football management – arrived to take the helm at champions Inter in 2008.

Juve did make a step forward – second, not third – but the goals had dried up as Trezeguet spent most of the campaign sidelined with a groin injury. Inter had enough about them – with a prime Zlatan Ibrahimovic banging in the goals – to continue their domestic dominance with Mourinho in charge, cruising to a fourth successive Scudetto with a 10-point lead.

Inter’s Portuguese coach was at his spikiest and most self-assured, refusing to shirk away from any verbal battles if he felt slighted by journalists or rival coaches.

Not for the first time, Ranieri found himself in Mourinho’s crosshairs during a wide-ranging rant at the media, Roma, Milan and Juve after a controversial decision to award Mario Balotelli a penalty in a 3-3 draw with Roma.

It has been revealed that “There has been the greatest amount of intellectual manipulation. There was a concerted, organised effort to manipulate public opinion. It was fantastic work but it is unrelated to my world – I work in football,” Mourinho claimed as Inter approached the finishing line in 2009.

“I don’t like intellectual prostitution, I like honesty. Over the last few days nobody has mentioned that Roma have great players but will end the season without a title. Nobody has mentioned that Milan have 11 fewer points than us and will end the season without a title.

It has been revealed that “Nobody has spoken about Juventus, who have won so many points thanks to refereeing mistakes. We have only won one game thanks to a mistake and that was the Siena match.

Industry observers note that “Ranieri remarked he is shoulder to shoulder with Luciano Spalletti? Well, I will side with all the coaches who have fallen foul against Juventus – Cesare Prandelli, Pasquale Marino, Gigi Del Neri.”.

Recent findings suggest that mourinho responded to the media, Spalleti and Ranieri who accused Mario Balotelli of being a diver, when Inter drew 3-3 with the Spalleti’s Roma. 🤯 pic.twitter.com/u3AeMPpVOs.

— Sir José #Giallorossi (@MourinhoTheGOAT) May 24, 2020.

Ranieri was sacked shortly before the end of the 2008-09 campaign after Juventus went tumbling out of the title race in a run of seven winless matches, while Mourinho signed a contract extension to commit his future at the San Siro.

As Mourinho was gearing up for a second season in charge, a rising Juventus, with Fabio Cannavaro making an ill-fated return following three years at the Bernabeu, were still being talked up as Inter’s likeliest challengers. Carlo Ancelotti and Kaka had left Milan, while Roma finished a distant sixth.

According to recent reports, luciano Spaletti had led Roma to the Supercoppa and Coppa Italia, as well a runner-up finish in Serie A, during the 2007-08 season, but they struggled to maintain the same standards the following year. After Roma started the 2009-10 season with back-to-back defeats to Genoa and Juve, Spaletti resigned.

In a recent development, after a summer off, Ranieri promptly found himself back in a job – at his hometown club, who he’d grown up supporting. But few if any pundits expected Roma to seriously compete with the journeyman coach at the helm – not least Mourinho, who evidently didn’t consider Ranieri a rival, every passing mention dripping with patronising contempt.

“Everyone knows that Ranieri is not a top-class coach, but he will not be expected to win the Scudetto. The target at the moment is middle-tier, so Roma have gone for a middle-tier coach,” wrote GOAL Italia’s editor Sergio Stanco in an op-ed reacting to the appointment.

And when the Giallorossi lost three Serie A matches in a row in late October in a series of fraught battles full of bookings and red cards, Roma found themselves down in 14th, two points clear of the relegation zone.

The only question was whether they could salvage a Europa League place, let alone mount a title push – Inter had started the season like a train and were 14 points clear after 10 matches.

What happened next, against all the odds, was one of the most thrilling and hard-fought title races that European football has ever seen.

READ: Comparing Claudio Ranieri’s eight best teams: Fiorentina, Chelsea, Leicester….

Slowly but surely, Ranieri’s Roma began to find form, holding table-topping Inter to a 1-1 draw at the San Siro as they kicked off a 24-match unbeaten run. Come to the winter break, they were up to fourth – but 11 points behind Mourinho’s league leaders.

Sources indicate that in the new year, Roma began to mix dazzling performances with gritty 1-0 wins. They looked like a title-winning side. Mirko Vucinic and Francesco Totti were routinely producing match-winning displays, while Daniele De Rossi was at the peak of his powers, looking every bit a world-class midfielder.

Sources indicate that ranieri’s men took 40 of the first 48 points available, winning 12 and drawing four, following the winter break. All the while Juventus were plummeting down to midtable obscurity since their decision to dismiss him.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Inter were faltering. Their comfortable lead was getting whittled away. They failed to win back-to-back matches between January and April and were constantly dropping points on their travels, failing to win at Bari, Parma, Napoli, Catania, Palermo and Fiorentina.

Come late March, and their visit to the Stadio Olimpico, Inter’s season looked on the verge of complete collapse. Mourinho’s man for the moment Diego Milito cancelled out De Rossi’s early opener, but Luca Toni – during a memorable half-season loan from Bayern Munich – came up with an iconic match-winner that resulted in one of the loudest roars in the history of the Eternal City. No Gladiator could muster a moment like this.

Industry observers note that FLASHBACK | 💥 | On this day in 2010… a classic finish from Luca Toni secured victory against Inter Milan! 👋#ASRoma pic.twitter.com/NjMdSyLaQs.

— AS Roma English (@ASRomaEN) March 27, 2018.

All season, Ranieri had played down his side’s chances of doing the impossible, just as he’d done at Juventus and just as he’d do at Leicester. But once Roma moved within a point of the top spot with seven games to go, the tinkerman allowed himself to dream.

“We’re out of the last bend and now we are on the final straight, one metre behind Inter,” said Ranieri after their 2-1 victory over Inter.

Sources indicate that “We have reopened the title race, now it will be a test of nerves. For five months we have chased and sacrificed ourselves to the cause; now we have beaten a stratospheric team who deserve our compliments.”.

An early Europa League exit to Panathinaikos at the first knockout hurdle allowed Roma to focus on domestic matters, while Inter were going deep into the Champions League.

Not only did the Giallorossi stand in Inter’s way in Serie A – even briefly usurping them to the top spot in April, with five games to go – but they were also their opponents in the Coppa Italia final.

But it was at this point, with their backs to the wall and in stark danger of crashing and burning, that Mourinho’s Inter did what the truly great sides do and stood up to produce some of their greatest performances when they needed to.

The counter-attacking masterclasses served to Barcelona and Bayern Munich in the semis and final of the Champions League were their most famous victories, but they were pushed to be every bit as good back home as the league and cup went down to the wire.

Milito, as he so often did in the defining games at the business end of Inter’s historic treble, came up with the decisive intervention and notched the only goal of the game in the Coppa final at the Olimpico, while a frustrated Totti was shown red in the dying moments.

After going top with three points against Atalanta, Ranieri’s Roma held onto their place at the summit the following week in a full-blooded derby against Lazio, peppered by 12 yellow cards and one red but most importantly a 2-1 win.

According to recent reports, but a week later they succumbed to a 2-1 defeat at home to Sampdoria. Totti had given Roma an early lead, but a second-half brace from Giampaolo Pazzini was enough to blow their title hopes. Just as you’d be brave to mention Steven Gerrard’s slip in the red half of Merseyside, Pazzini is a name best avoided in Rome.

In a recent development, iconic image of Mexes crying on the Roma bench was 10 years ago today. The infamous Roma-Samp pazzini game. The game that cost Roma the scudetto #ASRoma pic.twitter.com/R6yfaxo4eW.

— Scot Munroe (@scot_munroe) April 25, 2020.

It was Roma’s only defeat of their last 28 in Serie A, while they won eight of the last nine, but it was enough to cost them. Inter took advantage by winning their last five in a row, taking 19 of 21 points on offer after their defeat in the capital.

History is written by the victors, after all, leaving Roma to be remembered as one of the great nearly sides and Ranieri destined to be a nearly man – until Leicester, of course.

It was Ranieri’s miracle Foxes, after all, that inflicted a 2-1 victory on Mourinho’s Chelsea in December 2015, keeping them at the top of the table and their opponents just a point above the relegation zone.

Mourinho was then sacked, but – water under the bridge, apparently – he showed support to Ranieri following his dismissal at the King Power the following year, wearing CR on his training top in his press conference.

Industry observers note that ranieri returned to Roma for an emergency two-month spell at the end of the 2018-19 season. “Mr. Ranieri, in our moment of dire need, you have answered. Now, you receive the homage of your people,” read one banner and the veteran coach struggled to hold back the tears on the touchline in his first game back in charge at the Olimpico.

He later returned for a third stint, once again in their hour of need during the 2024-25 campaign.

Mourinho has since done something Ranieri never quite could and delivered silverware for the Giallorossi. But he never quite surpassed the love the Eternal City has for one of its favourite sons.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • St Mirren manager Craig McLeish claims self-interest and poor governance are killing Scottish football’s hopes of improvement.
  • McLeish is frustrated that Scottish Football Association chief football officer Craig Mulholland has reportedly had to dilute intends for young player quotas to appease five William Hill Premiership clubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026.

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish claims self-interest and poor governance are killing Scottish football’s hopes of improvement.

McLeish is frustrated that Scottish Football Association chief football officer Craig Mulholland has reportedly had to dilute intends for young player quotas to appease five William Hill Premiership clubs.

Mulholland was hoping to ensure teams featured Scotland Under-21 eligible players for an average of 60 minutes per league game and had two on the pitch for each cup tie.

McLeish stated: 'That’s damning that he’s having to change his prepares to pander to clubs who aren’t really on board with it and don’t really have the best interests of the Scottish national team at heart.

'I understand why. We have owners from outwith this country. We have managers from outwith this country. They’re in jobs, they’re all fighting for their clubs.

'But why then are those people allowed to be the ones that hold the keys to the future of our country and the development of our national team?

St Mirren boss Craig McLeish believes self-interest at clubs is hampering Scottish football.

'It’s the way governance is set up and we’ve killed ourselves with that because the people who actually have a say in it have, not have no interest but they’ve got self-interest, and there’s a lot of self-interest at the top end.

Sources indicate that 'I just don’t see a way that we can really properly change unless something to do with governance changes and I just don’t ever see that happening. It’s really sad.'.

Although McLeish backs quotas, he fears that would not address the root cause of Scottish football’s problems.

'We always focus at the top end, what our league size is, quotas for young players, a national base,' said the 36-year-old, who worked in St Mirren’s youth academy before his current role.

Sources indicate that 'We have a fundamental problem that starts at our youngest age groups, at four and five years of age, about how we actually teach kids to play. And until you fix that, you can’t fix the top end of it.

It has been revealed that 'It’s crazy some of the stuff that’s going on, the formats, how we teach kids. There’s just a massive lack of education and expertise at the very bottom of our pathway.

'In this country, football’s everyone’s sport and everyone gets access to it but if you take your young kids along to swimming or gymnastics or whatever other sport, you’re there with properly qualified coaches, teachers who have maybe done things at the top levels of that sport.

'We have nothing without the volunteers that work at the bottom end of the grassroots game, but they’re not teaching kids how to play football properly, in my mind.

'And you’re just hoping that they get put with a volunteer coach that can teach them something, that they get in with a really good group at the youngest ages.

'Because that development between the ages of three and eight, if you don’t get that right, you’re dead. You can’t do anything after that point, and we don’t do it well enough. And you’re just chasing yourself and we’ll never catch up.'.

The SFA has been contacted for comment.

Neil El Aynaoui has recovered from his injury and is ready to return to action for Leipzig.

The Moroccan midfielder, who left the national team’s training camp early due to leg problems, has received the green light from the German club’s medical staff.

According to BILD, the 2001-born player will be available to Martin Demichelis for the away match against Union Berlin, scheduled for Saturday, November 21st.

In a recent development, el Aynaoui had already resumed partial training with his teammates earlier this week, while sporting director Sebastian Schuppan had ruled out any serious problems in recent days: “It’s not a serious injury. It’s more of a combination of the games he’s played and the many knocks he’s received. He’s feeling the strain of the last few weeks and months.”.

The international break has therefore allowed him to recover without having to miss further matches against Leipzig.

The Moroccan has become a regular in Demichelis’s midfield, starting him in twelve of the thirteen matches played so far. His performances have also allowed him to leapfrog Nicolas Seiwald in the Argentine coach’s pecking order.

It has been revealed that according to BILD, if he continues at this level, a buyout at the end of the season could become a possibility. Leipzig paid Roma €4 million for the loan of El Aynaoui, with a buyout option set at €25 million.

Before deciding whether to acquire him permanently, however, the German club will also need to evaluate its own financial situation, given UEFA’s requirements regarding transfer revenue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Q: Jarrad, it’s still early in the season, but from your perspective, how is it going?

It’s going well. As a team, we’re in a positive place, especially after the recent results. It’s put us in a good position in the Cup and the Premier League.

Q: With how well it’s going in the league and the Carabao Cup, does it feel like there’s a lot of quality in this Everton squad?

I think the players we’ve got and the quality in the team is probably one of the best we’ve had over the past few seasons.

The squad isn’t as substantial as other squads, but the quality we have is definitely up there.

I think we’ve just got to stick together and be resilient.

Q: And after recovering from a hamstring injury last season, how are you feeling?

Good. I’m in a good position. I think the summer and pre-season helped to get me where I am now.

I was managed by staff, managed my load through pre-season, managed my training load.

So, hopefully, it’s helping. I'm feeling good.

Q: Just how frustrating was it last season?

It has been revealed that last season was tough. It was the first time I’d had a big injury which kept setting me back. When you can’t find a solution to something, it’s frustrating.

You do everything you can and then it sets you back again.

It has been revealed that Q: I remember you breaking down against Liverpool and you looked broken. That must’ve been horrible to deal with?

Yeah, I think it was the fourth time it had happened in the same place.

When you’ve tried different things and nothing’s happening, and then for [the injury] to happen again, it was tough.

It’s probably set me back a bit, so I’m trying to make up for the time I’ve lost. I think the start of the season has definitely helped with that.

According to recent reports, Q: What sort of approach did you take in your recovery? I imagine you tried several options.

I spoke to a few players who’ve had similar problems and reached out to someone in Germany – a specialist there – for a different approach to what I’d been doing, and the Club were on board with it.

I was there for four weeks, and they took me through their procedure, which looked – not just at the hamstring – but how the whole body moves, your brain and how everything moves.

It was a holistic approach and that definitely put me in a better position to come back here, and then with the Club helping me with my load, that put me in a better position.

Q: Are you able to share which other players you spoke to?

In a recent development, mainly Dominic Calvert-Lewin. When he was here, he was struggling with similar issues, so I reached out to him.

Tom Davies, as well. I reached out to him. They spoke really highly of [the specialist].

I spoke to Merlin (Röhl), and he knew a few people who had been there, so I think it was the right time to get different advice and a different opinion.

Q: But now, you’re feeling in a much better place?

Yeah, I feel in a better position now with the way I’ve been managed, and I feel confident in myself.

I think I feel more confident now coming back and I want to prove to everyone how good I am.

There are evenings which only accentuate doubts. The one experienced by Ferran Torres against Troyes on Saturday evening is undoubtedly one of them. In a meeting where Paris Saint-Germain ended up finding the fault to win (1-0), the Spanish striker, aligned in a right winger role, once again went through the debates without managing to be sufficiently decisive. However, there was no shortage of opportunities and opportunities to find the net presented themselves to him. But as too often in recent weeks, the last gesture was lacking. A new frustrating performance which extends a worrying period of scarcity for a player whose offensive efficiency is nevertheless one of the main missions.

Recent findings suggest that the Trojan evening did not allow Ferran Torres to smile again. From the 38th minute of play, the Spaniard came up against Hillel Konaté in a tight angle, before missing two new opportunities just before the break, in the 45th and 45th+2. In the second half, the scenario repeated itself: served by Fabián Ruiz in the 67th minute, he again saw the Trojan goalkeeper reject his attempt. Four clear chances, four failures and an exit in the 70th minute, replaced by Quentin Ndjantou. The contrast is striking with his Parisian debut: after scoring seven goals in his first six appearances, Torres is now going through a series of eight games without scoring.

As a reminder, his last goal dates back to September 20, during the victory against Olympique de Marseille in Ligue 1. In the Champions League, he has not found the net since his hat-trick against Slovan Bratislava. Faced with growing questions, Luis Enrique however chose to defend his attacker. Asked at a press conference about his difficulties, the Parisian coach, in fact, wanted to put this less good period into perspective: “everyone was concerned about Mika Godts, now it’s Ferran. These are attackers who miss and score goals.. A protective speech which reflects the technician’s desire not to publicly overwhelm his player.

In the mixed zone, Lucas Beraldo also recalled the importance of solidarity within the Parisian locker room, without wanting to dwell on the individual case of his teammate. “Torres? As I said, every match is different, tonight we played against a very good team, we managed to score and win and that’s the most vital thing. At PSG, we are a family, in good times and in bad times.. Valuable support for the Spaniard, who will now have to quickly regain his effectiveness. Because if Luis Enrique continues to place his trust in him, the missed opportunities begin to accumulate and the shortage becomes difficult to ignore.

Federico Chiesa could leave Liverpool as early as January, with Roma remaining among the clubs interested in bringing him back to Italy.

According to Calciomercato.com, the striker is considering a change of team to regain consistency, after another first half of the season spent almost entirely on the sidelines for the English club.

The 1997-born striker played just two minutes in the Premier League, coming on as a late substitute against Manchester City on October 11th.

Having arrived from Juventus in the summer of 2024, Chiesa has made 51 appearances and scored five goals for Liverpool, failing to secure a regular starting spot even after Andoni Iraola took over as manager.

It has been revealed that liverpool have so far asked for around €15 million for the player, ruling out the possibility of a loan, although the main obstacle for the Italian clubs is his €7.5 million per season salary. However, this could change in the coming months, given his contract expiring in June 2028 and the possibility that Chiesa agrees to spread his salary over a longer agreement.

Among the options reported is a three-year deal worth around €4 million annually. In addition to Roma, Inter Milan, Milan, and Napoli are also monitoring the former Juventus player, while possible destinations include Como and Lazio, and especially Saudi Arabia, where he would have a better chance of maintaining his current salary.

Breaking: Pocognoli's problems are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to those running the show at the SFA

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 10:30 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:25 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • For anyone with anything resembling a retentive memory, the alarm bells were going off all over the shop on the day Sebastien Pocognoli was unveiled as the newly introduced Scotland head coach.
  • Scottish Football Association (SFA) chief executive Ian Maxwell and chief football officer Craig Mulholland were there to crow about an extensive search of foreign fields to rival Captain Cook’s journeys around the Pacific and how data had helped land ‘one of Europe’s most sought-after coaches’ and secure the ‘aggressive, front-foot style of play’ that was going to bring a desired freshness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 10:30 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:25 EST, 20 November 2026.

For anyone with anything resembling a retentive memory, the alarm bells were going off all over the shop on the day Sebastien Pocognoli was unveiled as the newly introduced Scotland head coach.

Scottish Football Association (SFA) chief executive Ian Maxwell and chief football officer Craig Mulholland were there to crow about an extensive search of foreign fields to rival Captain Cook’s journeys around the Pacific and how data had helped land ‘one of Europe’s most sought-after coaches’ and secure the ‘aggressive, front-foot style of play’ that was going to bring a desired freshness.

Sources indicate that it was impossible to avoid the elephant in the room, though. Two-and-a-half months earlier, ahead of the disaster zone that was the World Cup, they’d handed Steve Clarke a fresh four-year contract.

According to recent reports, he was the polar opposite to Poco. Aggressive and front-foot, he most certainly wasn’t. The SFA knew Clarke didn’t have it in him to go for it at a major finals – as evidenced by two separate European Championship failures – but they decided to stick with the status quo anyway. Just as they did after Euro 2024, when he should have been sacked.

When Clarke finally did go of his own accord after the summer’s events in North America, Maxwell stated he was ‘sad’ the former Kilmarnock manager had stepped down and put a major dollop of blame on ‘some fairly hysterical commentary back home’.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland,  Pocognoli and SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell.

It just didn’t add up. How do you go from thinking a guy like Clarke is the future to tearing everything up, drafting in a London-based analytics firm to tell you who to go for as his replacement and coming up with a 39-year-old Belgian who wants to go for broke?

‘It doesn’t matter how you get there,’ offered Maxwell. ‘Let’s not get too hung up on the whys and the what-ifs.’.

Unfortunately, people are now starting to get hung up over the fact Pocognoli, for all the good on his CV, looks like he’s in the wrong movie – with his refusal to break from a failing three-at-the-back strategy suggesting a diploma from the Wilfried Nancy School of Intransigence ought to be on that resume too.

They are getting hung up on the fact captain Andy Robertson came out after the thrashing from Switzerland’s B-team to reveal the mood inside the camp has changed and warn there’s no breathing space to sort this out.

And they are getting hung up on the fact that it’s becoming considerably easier to reach the conclusion those above all of them at the very top of the SFA have never had a proper grip on things at all.

Clarke, of course, only exacerbated those concerns in September by expressing the view at a public event that Maxwell and Co ‘panicked a little bit’ in giving him that incomprehensible long-term deal because he’d threatened to announce he was quitting before the finals unless an agreement was reached.

In a recent development, ‘I wanted to control my narrative,’ he explained. It was hard to know who emerged from those admissions looking worse.

Clarke’s off the plot now, though, and it’s Maxwell, Mulholland and the SFA president Mike Mulraney left to try and convince us all that there is some kind of rhyme or reason to it all.

How things shape up with Pocognoli is an acid test for them. The rise or fall of a Scotland manager always hogs headlines. Yet, it is only one of a number of things coming together in what is starting to feel like a bit of a perfect storm.

Not so long ago, Maxwell and Mulholland were also yakking plenty about their statement project to increase game time for Scotland-eligible Under-21s.

It’s already in tatters, by the looks of things. The looks were watered down last month, without anything like the same fanfare, to involve Under-23 players and the intended votes on the proposals were pushed back.

A number of Premiership sides haven’t warmed to it and it remains to be seen whether it goes to a vote at all. Certainly, the radical change the top brass envisioned isn’t going to happen and that can only be regarded as an indicator that these guys running the game aren’t capable of taking it with them.

The start of Sebastien Pocognoli's reign has been concerning for Scotland fans.

It has been revealed that dundee manager Steven Pressley’s intervention over recent days hasn’t helped them either. After a long period on the outside looking in, Scotland have turned out in three major tournaments in the last five years.

Sources indicate that that has raised many millions of pounds, but the effect on elite level is questionable. Pressley talked of the sport being ‘built on sand’ as a result of there being no kind of national facility and you’d better believe it gained traction.

‘It says a lot about our strategy, our longevity and our long-term vision and we are finally seeing the effects of that. We have shown none of that over the period and it is all horribly catching up with us,’ he stated.

It has been revealed that the SFA do own Hampden, of course, thanks to that peculiar £5million deal from 2019 that involved Willie Haughey and Sir Tom Hunter ponying up half the money. Yet, how distant those days of Maxwell talking about taking examples from the way VfB Stuttgart revamped the Mercedes-Benz Arena and potentially implementing them in Mount Florida seem now.

Everyone appears to have given up on making the National Stadium better. Other problems have overtaken that old chestnut. Refereeing isn’t good enough. VAR isn’t up to scratch. General facilities require considerable improvement.

Should this Youth Strategy fail, there may also be a need for the SFA to look deeper within when addressing the dearth of top-tier talent coming through.

Industry observers note that it’s OK to blame clubs, but what about the level of coaching – and coach education – that exists at the national association? That’s before we even get to the ‘massive lack of expertise and education’ at the younger end of grassroots raised by St Mirren boss Craig McLeish.

Sources indicate that the SFA set-up for producing coaches was once the envy of many. We all remember Jose Mourinho and others at the Largs finishing school. Now? Even Maxwell, after stating there were no viable Scottish rivals to Pocognoli for the Scotland job, admitted the coaching pathway needs looked at.

Industry observers note that there is only one problem here, though. Maxwell has been the chief executive since May 2018. He’s in his ninth year in the role. What has he really achieved? What have his big ideas been?

Recent findings suggest that yes, Scotland made it back to major finals under Clarke, but Clarke was a painfully obvious choice to be made national coach in 2019. He’d worked wonders at Rugby Park and did transfer that to the international scene until it came to actually turning out in those showpiece competitions.

Now they’ve had to get creative, there is so much hanging on Pocognoli’s reign for the guys at the top.

Recent findings suggest that maxwell was a bloke who landed in the role of Partick Thistle GM almost by mistake after failing to beat Jackie McNamara to the manager’s job. Just before leaving for the SFA, the Jags got relegated.

Talk of redeveloping Hampden has gone quiet as other problems take the spotlight.

At his Hampden unveiling, he had to fend off questions about only getting that position through behind-the-scenes politicking and insist he wouldn’t be a puppet for anyone.

Mulholland also seems a surprising choice as the architect of the national sport’s renovation. He spent two decades in the Rangers academy and eight years as head of it.

Industry observers note that has it been a conveyor belt of talent for the Ibrox first-team? Do you recall much wailing and gnashing of teeth when he left in 2023 amid a wider changing of the guard?

Then, there’s Mulraney, the former Alloa chairman and SFA director for over a decade.

It has been revealed that you don’t see much of him these days. Maybe because people want to ask about his position as chair of FIFA’s finance committee in the wake of the most greed-infested World Cup ever and the ongoing soap opera surrounding Gianni Infantino. But maybe not.

How things work out with Pocognoli might end up being the one thing that puts all these guys under the kind of examination that cannot be bodyswerved, but it’s only the tip of the iceberg.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Time is a curse for a football fan, as a host of players we have watched for major periods of their career call it a day and hang up their boots.
  • We’ve looked into 18 players who have called it a day in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well-known former Chelsea, Barcelona and Liverpool players are among the massive names to have retired in 2026.

Time is a curse for a football fan, as a host of players we have watched for major periods of their career call it a day and hang up their boots.

We’ve looked into 18 players who have called it a day in 2026.

Berahino has retired from football at 33 to concentrate on his role as a coach with Burundi’s national team.

It feels like a long time ago that he scored 20 goals in league and cup for West Brom in 2014-15. That made Berahino hot property, with Spurs seriously keen before plumping for Son Heung-min instead.

The striker never did capture that form again, faltering with the Baggies before a disastrous £12 million move to Stoke in 2017.

Berhaino has since played for Charlton and Sheffield Wednesday, before spells in Cyprus, India and Slovenia.

Pedro ends his playing career as one of the most decorated players in modern football, having won the World Cup and Euros with Spain alongside a plethora of trophies at club level.

The forward was part of Pep Guardiola’s glittering Barcelona side, before scoring 43 goals in 206 Chelsea appearances.

He left to join Roma in 2020, before becoming the first player since 1985 to move between the two Rome rivals when he signed for Lazio in the following year.

Pedro remained at Lazio until his decision to retire at the age of 39.

After a glittering career, including World Cup glory in 2014 and 49 goals for Germany, Podolski called it a day in May 2026.

The 40-year-old represented several European giants throughout his career, including Bayern Munich, Inter Milan, Galatasaray and Arsenal.

He ended his career with boyhood club Gornik Zabrze in Poland and even skippered them to cup glory in his final campaign.

Borini played for Chelsea and Liverpool in the early-2010s, but is still beloved at Sunderland for his relegation-dodging goals under Gus Poyet and Sam Allardyce.

Industry observers note that the forward left Wearside in 2018, spending time in exotic locations like Milan, deepest Turkey and Salford. He retired in October 2026.

Former Arsenal, Swansea and West Ham goalkeeper Fabianski has hung up his gloves at the age of 41.

But Fabianski has no intention of quitting the game entirely, announcing his looks to work with the next generation of goalkeepers in a coaching role.

No Premier League player has ever made more appearances than Milner, who broke Gareth Barry’s long-standing record in February 2026.

The midfielder made his Leeds debut in 2002, sharing a pitch with sepia-toned names like Nigel Winterburn and Lucas Radebe.

His career with Leeds, Aston Villa, Newcastle, Manchester City, Liverpool, Brighton and England was nothing less than stellar and Milner called it a day this year at the age of 40.

started his career at Cardiff City before a 2008 move to Arsenal, where he won three FA Cups – scoring the winning goal in two of those finals – during his 11 years with the Gunners.

He then had spells with Juventus, Nice, Rangers, a second stint at Cardiff and Pumas UNAM before ending his career in April.

Ramsey is now manager of League One side Oxford United.

One of the biggest sh*thouses in recent football history, Costa was a menace during his days with Atletico Madrid and Chelsea.

He played his last professional match in 2024, but it wasn’t until earlier this year when he appeared on a podcast that he confirmed his retirement.

Oscar was just 25 when he signed for Shanghai Port, leaving Chelsea for a £60million fee and plenty of raised eyebrows.

The Brazilian spent seven years in China to the glee of his bank manager, although a player of such talent should really have been playing in a more competitive league.

He spent the last few months of his career at Sao Paulo, before retiring in April. This was due to a heart condition which led to him collapsing and requiring CPR in a training session.

Young brought the curtain down on an exceptional 23-year career in May, retiring at the age of 40 after a final season with Ipswich Town in the Championship.

Starting as a winger with Watford and Aston Villa, Young gradually became a defender during his Manchester United days and won a Serie A title with Inter Milan in 2021.

He was also an important member of England’s 2018 World Cup squad.

One of the biggest ‘Streets Won’t Forget’ footballers in Premier League history after his spell at West Ham in the mid-2010s, Payet retired earlier this year.

Industry observers note that the French playmaker spent the final years of his playing days at Vasco de Gama, still capable of scoring outrageous free-kicks. A maverick in an increasingly systemised sport.

Most famously associated with Leicester’s 2016 title win, Schmeichel retired in May 2026 after suffering a shoulder injury a few months previously.

Then with Celtic, it was expected that Schemeichel’s surgery would keep him out of action for up to a year anyway.

Aged 39, the son of legendary goalkeeper Peter enjoyed a hugely successful career in his own right.

A loyal servant at Chelsea between 2012 and 2023, Azpilicueta ended his career in May after helping Sevilla avoid relegation.

The full-back made over 500 appearances for Chelsea, the sixth most in the club’s history, and appeared as a BBC pundit during the World Cup.

An eight-times capped Netherlands international, Van Ginkel represented major clubs like Chelsea and AC Milan, but his careers at both clubs were short.

In England, he also played for Stoke, but the midfielder featured in his home country for the majority of his career, playing more than 100 games for both PSV Eindhoven and Vitesse.

At 33 years of age, Van Ginkel has hung up his boots.

Pjanic had a very successful career at club level, playing for giants such as Roma, Juventus and Barcelona.

The Bosnian won seven trophies with Juve, one with Barca and was named Roma’s footballer of the year in 2014.

At international level, he’ll go down as a legend, having represented his country over 100 times, while he contributed to two goals in his three World Cup games.

Pjanic technically retired in the final days of 2025, but who cares for such semantics? Any excuse for us to relive his glory days at Lyon.

Sakho left Paris Saint-Germain for a Liverpool team which wasn’t particularly good while he was there, and in doing so ended his spell of winning trophies: four at PSG and not a single one in his career after that.

The Reds finished second in Sakho’s first campaign there, before slipping to sixth and then eighth in the Premier League for the following two seasons.

Sakho was on the club’s books as they finished fourth the next season, though he was on loan at Crystal Palace when that happened.

He would move permanently to Palace, netting Liverpool a healthy fee, then back to France with Montpellier, before his final spell in professional football with Torpedo Kutaisi in Georgia.

Mata finished his career playing in Australia, leaving Melbourne Victory in September before confirming his retirement in November.

The Spaniard starred for Chelsea and Manchester United in the Premier League in his prime after coming through the Real Madrid academy and making his name at Valencia.

A World Cup winner with Spain in 2010 and a member of their triumphant Euro 2012 squad, Mata is now bowing out at the age of 38.

A three-time Europa League winner with Sevilla, Banega was clearly eager not to just be remembered as the guy who ran over his own foot at a petrol station.

The midfielder had a 10-year international career with Argentina and was most recently playing back in his homeland with Defensa y Justicia.

But at the age of 38, he’s saying enough is enough. “Even if Messi calls me for Inter Miami, I would tell him no,” insisted Banega, who also remarked he wouldn’t want to “take the place” of young players trying to break through at clubs.

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice noted, and that summed it up succinctly.

Sources indicate that and that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”.

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Industry observers note that vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

Sources indicate that for Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. Roma are back in the hunt for Samuel Lino, this time reportedly ready to offer €45 million.

According to RTI Esporte, the Giallorossi have initiated new contacts with the Brazilian winger’s representatives, expressing their willingness to invest a significant sum to bring him to the capital during the January transfer window.

The sum would be higher than the €25 million Flamengo had already rejected, according to rumors circulating in recent weeks.

The Rio club hasn’t ruled out a move away, but continues to demand high prices for the 1999-born player, so much so that ESPN Brasil had indicated a valuation close to €60 million, corresponding to the player’s release clause.

Flamengo’s financial situation could favor negotiations, especially after the suspension of their sponsorship agreement with Betano, which guaranteed the club up to 268.5 million reais per season.

The contract has been suspended until March 31, 2027, barring any further developments, and the Brazilian club is evaluating how to compensate for the shortfall, including through possible transfers.

Samuel Lino arrived at Flamengo in the summer of 2025 from Atlético Madrid in a deal worth approximately €22 million plus bonuses. This season, he has made 54 appearances, scoring 15 goals and providing 13 assists.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that philippe Diallo is launching into a major battle. The president of the French Football Federation (FFF) has decided to run for the presidency of Fifa, with the ambition of succeeding Gianni Infantino next March. Already supported by UEFA, the French leader is now seeking to convince the various federations. With this in mind, he will travel to Abuja, Nigeria, on Saturday, where the General Assembly of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) will be held.

A trip far from trivial. Philippe Diallo knows it, the African continent constitutes particularly favorable terrain for Gianni Infantino. The outgoing president benefits from significant support, which his opponent intends to try to change. But this strategy is far from unanimous. On social networks, Romain Molina strongly criticized the first choices of the French candidate and the way in which his entourage intends to campaign.

The independent journalist, although an opponent of Gianni Infantino, does not mince his words. According to him, Philippe Diallo and certain UEFA officials are completely wrong in their approach to African football. “Either Philippe Diallo is very, very poorly advised, or has he not understood the dynamics of Fifa and international football? His start to the campaign is a sketch since everyone, including several UEFA leaders, is focusing on Africa, which is nonsense, believing that the French-European networks will help (getting 15 votes in Africa would be a victory because it would allow us not to lose the election there). Ideas from another time, with the thought of bringing in well-known people (Africans in particular) to support his campaign and go to large countries with a French-speaking majority (which is the worst possible idea given the arrogance associated with France and UEFA, an elitist association which does not care about “others”)”he believes.

Romain Molina denounces in particular a lack of understanding of the balance of power within international bodies and African federations. The journalist continues his charge by directly implicating the entourage of the president of the FFF. “How can you be so disconnected from reality? However, is this surprising given the recycled “advisors” around him? These people have NO idea of ​​the reality of the federations affiliated to Fifa, and even less of the current dynamics within the confederations/sub-confederations. » A particularly severe first warning for Philippe Diallo, who will have to convince well beyond his European supporters if he wants to shake Gianni Infantino.

#60179. Tech Report: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts.
  • Locusts are infamous for their ability to form giant swarms that can devastate plants, including crops, across vast areas1.
  • Three years ago, we discovered an anti-cannibalism pheromone — an odorous chemical (odorant) that conveys a message between members of a species — that protects migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) from being eaten3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a summary of: Han, W. et al. Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11297-7 (2026).

Locusts are infamous for their ability to form giant swarms that can devastate plants, including crops, across vast areas1. One of the forces thought to drive swarms of young, flightless locusts in the ‘hopper’ life stage is cannibalism: individuals at the back eat those in front if they fail to move fast enough. Cannibalism is thus an important factor that underpins the collective behaviour of locusts2.

Three years ago, we discovered an anti-cannibalism pheromone — an odorous chemical (odorant) that conveys a message between members of a species — that protects migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) from being eaten3. We wanted to know whether other odorants might act as attractants. We had observed that wounded locusts were particularly likely to be attacked and consumed, so we started our investigation there.

Sources indicate that initially, we used behavioural experiments to investigate whether hungry locusts are indeed attracted to wounded individuals of the same species (Fig. 1). Next, we collected odorants emitted by wounded locusts and performed chemical analyses to identify attractive compounds, which we then tested in further behavioural experiments. Earlier work had shown that the odorants we identified are produced by bacteria living in or on locusts4, so we asked whether bacteria were responsible for producing them in injured locusts as well.

Figure 1 | Locust cannibals devouring a wounded locust. Four migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) in the fifth-instar (final) developmental stage attack and devour a wounded fourth-instar individual of the same species.Credit: Han, W. et al./Nature (CC BY 4.0).

For an odorant to function as a cue, it must first be detected. We therefore investigated the locust’s smell-sensing (olfactory) system, located in the antennae, and found receptor proteins that detect the compound we had identified. Using gene editing, we knocked out the genes that encode these receptors to investigate their role in attracting cannibals. We also disrupted odorant production in the implicated bacteria. To understand why wounded locusts emit these odorants, we used various behavioural and molecular methods to investigate changes in the expression of genes involved in the locust immune system.

Our experiments revealed that bacteria that proliferate around wounds in locusts produce the odorant guaiacol (which smells like single-malt whisky). It is detected by receptor proteins in the antennae of other locusts, attracting potential cannibals. Guaiacol also activates the immune system of the wounded locust, helping to protect the wound against infection by disease-causing agents (pathogens).

Sources indicate that at the relatively low concentrations typically associated with small wounds, the compound did not attract cannibals, and the wound often healed. However, at higher concentrations, guaiacol reached levels that attracted other locusts, leading to the wounded insect being attacked and eaten. The system therefore involves a trade-off between fighting pathogens and attracting hungry members of the same species.

The processes that underlie the formation and movement of giant locust swarms remain unclear. However, by revealing a trade-off between immunity and cannibalism, we have added another piece to the puzzle. A deeper understanding of chemical communication in locusts might also inform the development of environmentally sustainable approaches to locust management. More broadly, the finding that a bacterially produced compound can act as a signal to activate genes involved in the immune system is interesting from biological and medical perspectives.

The main limitation of our study is that we have not yet uncovered the mechanism by which particular bacteria are recruited to wound sites. How does the number of bacteria increase, and how do they populate the wound?

Recent findings suggest that the natural next step is to conduct experiments addressing these questions. By introducing specific markers, such as fluorescent proteins, into the bacteria, it should be possible to track their movement through the body and investigate their distribution across organs before and after a locust is wounded. — Hetan Chang and Bill S. Hansson are at the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Shenzhen, China. B.S.H. is also at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology, Jena, Germany.

“This paper describes how cannibalistic behaviour in a migratory locust is stimulated by recruitment of symbiotic bacteria to an injury site, where the bacteria release a volatile chemical perceived by conspecifics as an indicator of an incapacitated peer, triggering cannibalistic consumption. The work is extremely convincing, and the underlying biology is exciting. The combination of approaches the authors use to determine the basis for the attraction and cannibalistic behaviour is outstanding.” — Brian Lazarro is at Cornell University, Ithaca, Latest York, USA.

In a recent development, we are fascinated by insects and especially by swarming locusts. What holds a swarm together? Which mechanisms drive it forward? How do individuals interact in the swarm? And how does the swarm eventually break down into individuals? When we discovered the anti-cannibalism pheromone3, we wondered whether there might also be attractant odorants that prompt locusts to attack one another. When we observed that wounded locusts were often attacked, we decided to collect odorants specifically from them. A key moment came when we realized that guaiacol was produced not by locusts, but by bacteria. This meant that we could identify the guaiacol-producing bacteria and determine which biochemical pathways they used. We were accustomed to studying pheromones produced by moths, flies and beetles. Here, however, we had an animal carrying a microbiome-based odorant factory. When we discovered that the odorant also boosted immune function in the wounded animal, our eyes were opened even wider. — B.S.H.

According to recent reports, at low concentrations, a chemical called guaiacol prompts locusts to flock together, and encourages pathogen resistance and healing. Synthesized by a bacterial symbiont, Enterobacter hormaechi, higher concentrations turn locusts nasty, prompting them to eat their wounded comrades, overcoming the cannibalism-suppressing pheromone phenylacetonitrile. — Henry Gee, Senior Editor, Nature.

Roma is ready to return to action after the international break.

The Giallorossi will fly to the Tardini to face Alberto Gilardino’s Parma, who spoke on the eve of the match about his relationship with the Grugliasco-born coach. The Giallorossi coach spoke at a press conference one day before the match against Parma.

It has been revealed that “Dybala and Svilar trained well. They have fully recovered. Pellegrini, who will have a longer return, and Rensch, who has started training with good intensity, are left out.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Last year’s comeback against Parma was crucial; it opened the doors to the Champions League for us. It was a fundamental step. This fresh season is different; the objectives are emerging along the way.”.

Sources indicate that “As for the transfer market, it’s appropriate for the CEO to speak about it. If necessary, he’ll be the one to say what Roma can do on the market, which is always a complicated and difficult one.”.

According to recent reports, “Soule? Clearly, travel and time zones have an impact. We’ll try to figure it out this afternoon during the final training session, including for Balerdi and Castro. We left Soulé in extraordinary condition, but we have three vital matches. Soulé isn’t a problem; the important thing is that he’s injury-free.”.

“Dybala? I don’t know his condition. We’ll see what happens as we play. It’s true he hasn’t played for a month, but sooner or later he’ll have to play, and we’ll evaluate him during the match. He’s recovered physically, so we’ll see how he’s doing from time to time.”.

It has been revealed that “Having Soulé and Dybala at our disposal is a strength. Soulé has reached a high level of quality, he’s been called up to the Argentina squad. He’s evolving, like Mora. They’re players who are growing, the important thing is to have them. Dybala and Soulé are a great fit; coexistence is a false problem.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the strength of the squad, despite the many absences. “We’ve had strong performances from other players, which have helped us avoid feeling the impact of the absences. We have to look ahead; the break always leaves you with some doubts. You think you can restart with the certainties of Sassuolo, but that’s not the case. There have been constant breaks lately, and some players have played less. So it’s also an individual assessment, especially regarding the first matchday. We need to get back on track immediately. Tomorrow is a tough match; the standings are starting to become more clear, and points are starting to count for more.”.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think there are any definitive transfer market situations today. There are still a lot of games to go, and players who aren’t playing can play more, or vice versa. We’re in constant conversation with D’Amico, but there’s been no transfer planning other than between the two of us.”.

  • In his first sit-down interview in five months, Berrada tackled topics ranging from the relationship between the Glazers and Ineos, the imminent departure of youngster JJ Gabriel, the decision not to sign a left back in the summer, as well as the decision to push ahead for a new stadium despite supporter backlash on matchdays.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 10:25 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:32 EST, 20 November 2026.

Manchester United CEO Omar Berrada insists the team got 'fundamentally better' after this summer's transfer window, as he warned ‘spending just for the sake of it’ is not the route to putting United back on top.

In his first sit-down interview in five months, Berrada tackled topics ranging from the relationship between the Glazers and Ineos, the imminent departure of youngster JJ Gabriel, the decision not to sign a left back in the summer, as well as the decision to push ahead for a new stadium despite supporter backlash on matchdays.

The United chief has been at the centre of furious protests and anti-ownership chanting at matches this season, alongside Director of Football Jason Wilcox, and he accepted that criticism of United's leadership has, mostly, been fair.

In an interview that aired shortly after upcoming head coach Mauricio Pochettino spoke to the media for the first time, Berrada was pressed on how much accountability falls at his door with United heading to Anfield this weekend 18th in the Premier League table.

'I think if you think about the fact we've had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven't achieved the stability that we wanted, that's for sure,' Berrada told Sky Sports.

'When it doesn't work out with the coach or the manager, we are all responsible. Myself, the football leadership, everyone who is involved around the coach and the staff and the players. We have to continue improving and getting better.

Manchester United's CEO Omar Berrada finally fronted up in an interview with Sky Sports.

Michael Carrick's sacking was yet another managerial change at United, with the hierarchy under massive scrutiny and Mauricio Pochettino now in the hotseat.

'There are different circumstances why it didn't work out with Erik [ten Hag], and Ruben [Amorim], and now Michael [Carrick], and we are always learning and, as I remarked, trying to improve and understand what has failed.

'The challenge is we're trying to find the right manager for the squad that we have with a specific set of skills in that moment to make them perform at their best level.

In a recent development, 'It's true, we have to accept the criticism that we haven't been able to achieve that stability with one coach and our aim is to do that as soon as possible. Of course, we hope now that Mauricio coming in will give us that stability that I think we all need.'.

Berrada's links to Manchester City, where he worked prior to joining United, were brought up, not least given he worked at the club during the period that City have had charges brought against them.

'I'm not concerned,' Berrada insisted.

But at his new home there are issues aplenty, not least having got another managerial appointment wrong, sacking Carrick less than six months after handing him a two-year deal, and so it was put to Berrada: is the club actually progressing?

'It's not good enough, not acceptable and that's why we've made the change that we made so that we can move forward,' he concluded.

(L-R) Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Berrada and Jason Wilcox have drawn plenty of ire from Man United fans.

Sources indicate that 'But we are laying the foundations for sustained growth, to put us in a position where we can be competitive consistently. It's not always been that.

'Last year we finished third, we were happy with the squad, we were happy with the way we were going. And now, a few months later, we are not where we need to be. But the foundations are there and I am convinced that we are heading in the right direction. Very positive.'.

Breaking: 6 times players came back to haunt their old club ahead of Bruno Guimaraes’ Newcastle return

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bruno Guimaraes is the latest Premier League player to return to a former club as Arsenal take on Newcastle United, but will the Brazilian follow in the footsteps of others and get a goal?
  • From apologising to full-length runs of the pitch, players scoring against their old clubs results in a number of different reactions.
  • Here are six of the best of them from Premier League history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bruno Guimaraes is the latest Premier League player to return to a former club as Arsenal take on Newcastle United, but will the Brazilian follow in the footsteps of others and get a goal?

From apologising to full-length runs of the pitch, players scoring against their old clubs results in a number of different reactions.

Here are six of the best of them from Premier League history.

We’re generally against players not celebrating goals against former clubs but when that player has played 648 times for them, perhaps we can understand it.

Lampard’s move from Chelsea to Upcoming York City came with an unexpected stopping-over point of Manchester City where of course he scored against his former club.

It was at the Etihad and City were trailing thanks to a goal from Andre Schurrle when Lampard scored an equaliser five minutes from time.

He looked like a dog that had just eaten something he knows he shouldn’t have as he put a single hand up in the air to apologise.

Rooney’s departure from Everton was a little messy with Everton fans chanting against him even as he was still their player and that bitterness was still there three years later.

In 2007, United trailed Everton 2-0 which gave the home fans the confidence to give their old player a bit of stick.

But it was a case of kicking the bear. United levelled in the 68th minute after Phil Neville put the ball in his own net and 11 minutes from time, Rooney grabbed the winner.

And there was certainly no lack of a celebration.

After a few bounces like a man who could not decide what to do, Rooney looked the Goodison Park faithful in the eye and kissed the United badge.

Would Wayne Rooney have worked in Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona?

It is the absolute gold standard of blood-boiling celebrations.

Adebayor was annoyed at Arsenal for what he felt was Arsene Wenger forcing him out, resulting in a £25.5m move to Manchester City.

Wenger suggested it was more a need to raise money but Adebayor took it to heart and let his emotions come out when the two clubs next met.

Sources indicate that he netted in a 4-2 win and sprinted the full length of the pitch to taunt the travelling Arsenal fans. Referee Mark Clattenburg looked like a disappointed parent while stewards struggled to hold the enraged Arsenal fans back.

It was not Adebayor’s only moment of the game either. He stamped on Robin van Persie’s face, landing him a retrospective three-match ban, and even got into arguments with Cesc Fabregas and Alex Song.

Ince had controversially made his way to Liverpool having previously spent six years at United and he rubbed salt into the wound in 1999.

A few weeks before United would go on to lift the treble, Ince scored a late equaliser at Anfield and celebrated by hugging about six different fans in the stands.

The goal and result looked to have swung the title race to Arsenal but United did eventually lift the trophy.

Van Persie was enemy number one around the Emirates in 2012 after he left for Manchester United and he acknowledged that fact when he scored in the first three minutes when they met at Old Trafford in the 2012/13 season.

In a recent development, he gave a double-handed apology and looked genuinely disheartened by the goal. In the away leg, he scored once more but again refused to celebrate.

Six months on though and Van Persie very much did celebrate.

Recent findings suggest that he rose well to meet a Wayne Rooney corner and went full knee slide in his celebration. As he was hugging Rooney, his face did though look like a man who’s just remembered he was supposed to not celebrate.

It’s not one of the more well-known names but we are including it because it led to a rule change.

LuaLua was on loan at Portsmouth from Newcastle at a time when there was no restriction on when loan players could feature.

Newcastle were winning 1-0 away at Fratton Park when guess who scored to equalise it. Bearing in mind he was still an employee at this point, LuaLua celebrated by taking his shirt off in what is possibly the furthest thing away from an apology.

Newcastle manager Bobby Robson remarked: “He was the last player we wanted to score against us. One of our players has taken a point off us.”.

That bizarre situation led to the Premier League tweaking the rules to prevent loaned players from facing their parent club.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roma have found an additional weapon in their defenders to fuel the best attack in Serie A, with eight of the 31 goals scored so far this season coming from their back line.

According to recent reports, as La Gazzetta dello Sport points out, their contribution accounts for 26% of Gasperini’s team’s overall goals, with Hermoso, Balerdi, and Lulli each contributing two, while Ndicka and Ghilardi have each scored one. Including their nine assists, the defenders’ total contribution to goals rises to 17, almost double that of Inter and Lazio, both with nine.

This figure confirms the importance of the back line in the Giallorossi’s attacking output, as they consistently involve the center backs in creating chances and making runs into the opponent’s penalty area.

Recent findings suggest that the performance of the Giallorossi defenders is unmatched even in the major European leagues, where only Luis Enrique’s PSG have scored more goals from their defensive line, with nine. The French side, Roma’s next opponents in the Champions League, are one point ahead of Gasperini’s team, while Atlético Madrid are behind them with seven goals, Mainz, Stuttgart, and Brighton with five.

The basis of these numbers is Gasperini’s system, which requires defenders to drop forward and participate consistently in the attacking phase.

The wing-backs often accompany the play into the attacking midfield, seeking space to insert themselves and create numerical superiority. Curiously, Gianluca Mancini, one of the players who most often plays this role, is still missing from the scorers’ charts, but he hasn’t scored in the league so far.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As Il Romanista reports, excavations for the archaeological surveys have been completed, and the relevant documentation has already been submitted to the Superintendency, from which approval is awaited.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The construction process for AS Roma’s new stadium in Pietralata continues, with the Giallorossi club working on the final adjustments to the detailed design, expected by Christmas.

As Il Romanista reports, excavations for the archaeological surveys have been completed, and the relevant documentation has already been submitted to the Superintendency, from which approval is awaited.

This marks another step toward the start of construction, with the spring 2027 target confirmed. Massimiliano Umberti, president of the 4th Municipality of Rome, spoke to Radio Romanista.

When asked about the completion of the excavations, Umberti replied: “Yes, from what I know, yes. We are waiting for the PES from AS Roma, then there will be the tender for the areas. And then, finally, I think April could be the right month for the first stone.”.

There’s also news regarding the proposal to name the current Quintiliani Metro B stop, located near the area designated for the fresh facility, after Dino Viola. The motion, presented by Councilor Riccardo Corbucci and co-signed by Ubaldo Righetti and Federico Rocca, has been tabled and awaits discussion in the Capitoline Assembly. Umberti reiterated his desire to link the neighborhood to the Giallorossi’s history: “There’s no point in hiding it: the IV Municipio will be branded Rome for obvious reasons.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Everton tasted their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup as the Blues' four-game winning streak in the competition came to its conclusion with a 2-1 defeat away to Manchester United.
  • First half strikes from Mared Griffiths and Emma Watson put the Red Devils in to a two-goal lead, before Noemie Mouchon halved the deficit two minutes after the break.
  • Prior to Wednesday night's clash, the Toffees had comfortably beaten Birmingham City, Newcastle United and Sheffield United before thrashing Durham 6-0 in the competition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton tasted their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup as the Blues' four-game winning streak in the competition came to its conclusion with a 2-1 defeat away to Manchester United.

First half strikes from Mared Griffiths and Emma Watson put the Red Devils in to a two-goal lead, before Noemie Mouchon halved the deficit two minutes after the break.

Prior to Wednesday night's clash, the Toffees had comfortably beaten Birmingham City, Newcastle United and Sheffield United before thrashing Durham 6-0 in the competition.

Head coach Scott Phelan named a heavily-rotated XI from the side that were held to a goalless draw against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday.

Rylee Foster-Inman started in between the sticks, with Issy Hobson making her first appearance in two months in front of her.

Up top, Mouchon led the line after netting a brace in the Blues’ 6-0 demolition of Durham seven days ago.

Sources indicate that foster-Inman produced a fine save when faced one-on-one with Griffiths inside six minutes. The keeper rushed out upon recognising the danger and did brilliantly to narrow the angle.

The shot-stopper denied Griffiths once more on 21 minutes as the youngster pulled the trigger from the edge of the box after a cute turn saw her evade Hobson.

According to recent reports, the lively Griffiths was in the thick of the action once more in the 34th minute as United came inches away from opening the scoring. Rebecca Bernal burst forward to meet her in swinging cross, the Mexican’s header sailing just over.

Sources indicate that griffiths would not be denied only 60 seconds later as the forward broke the deadlock in style. She sprinted down the left before chopping past Finnigan and firing past the outrushed Foster-Inman.

Watson then doubled the hosts’ lead on the stroke of half-time. Ella Toone wrong-footed Finnigan before pulling it back to the former-Blue. Watson finished emphatically from close range, with that concluding the action for the opening 45.

Defensive duo Hobson and Silcock made way for Hannah Blundell and Rion Ishikawa at the break.

Recent findings suggest that everton halved the deficit only 60 seconds after the restart as Mouchon netted her third goal from her last two Cup appearances. Quick feet from Vignola allowed the Spaniard room to free Hannah Cain down the right. The Wales international then squared it to the advancing Mouchon, who finished off the post.

Maz Pacheco then came agonisingly close from 20-yards out as her wicked free-kick rattled the upright. The full-back picked her spot from the set-piece – the ball crashing against the crossbar with the keeper well-beaten.

Phelan then made two further changes on 68 minutes as Ruby Mace and Hikaru Kitagawa replaced Clare Wheeler and Vignola.

With eight minutes remaining, Naomi Layzell – who claimed the Player of the Match award when the two sides met in the WSL – came on in place of Aurora Galli.

Despite a late push for an equaliser, United stood firm and succumbed the Toffees to their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup.

Everton return to Goodison Park on Sunday afternoon (2pm KO) as Brighton & Hove Albion travel to L4.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Industry observers note that back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

It has been revealed that fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

It has been revealed that now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on November 20, 2010, Tottenham Hotspur played their part in one of the most memorable North London derbies in history with a 3-2 comeback victory over Arsenal.
