Tech Report: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a summary of: Guerrero-Ramírez, N.
  • Tropical rainforests contain extraordinary biodiversity, but large areas have been converted into agricultural plantations.
  • We surveyed 24 groups of organisms, including plants, birds, bats, arthropods, soil animals and microorganisms, and recorded roughly 40,000 species across a gradient of land-use intensification in Sumatra, Indonesia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a summary of: Guerrero-Ramírez, N. R. et al. Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11298-6 (2026).

Tropical rainforests contain extraordinary biodiversity, but large areas have been converted into agricultural plantations. This transformation is often accompanied by farming intensification, in which diverse vegetation is replaced by monocultures to increase production1. Losses of local species because of such intensified practices are well documented, but less is known about how agriculture alters the composition of biological communities across landscapes. One possible outcome is biotic homogenization, in which intensive land use makes these communities in agricultural sites increasingly similar to each other, compared with those of forests. Conversely, they might become more dissimilar in species composition in agricultural lands — called biotic differentiation. However, distinct groups of organisms might respond in contrasting ways that are not captured by measuring changes in the total number of species, or species richness. Understanding how biodiversity changes within and between sites is crucial for designing agricultural landscapes that reconcile farming with biodiversity conservation2.

We surveyed 24 groups of organisms, including plants, birds, bats, arthropods, soil animals and microorganisms, and recorded roughly 40,000 species across a gradient of land-use intensification in Sumatra, Indonesia. The sites ranged from tropical lowland forests and traditional rubber agroforests (in which rubber trees grow alongside other vegetation) to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures of rubber and oil palm. We could therefore test similarities and differences in biodiversity responses to various types of land use in this hyper-biodiverse region. We distinguished between changes within multi-taxon communities that arise from species replacement, and variation because of species-poor communities that contain subsets of the species found at richer sites.

We found marked biodiversity losses with agricultural intensification. Compared with forests, monocultures had around 50% lower local multidiversity (average species richness across the 24 groups) and 78% lower landscape-level multidiversity. Notably, traditional rubber agroforests retained many forest-associated species that were absent from monocultures (Fig. 1).

In a recent development, figure 1 | Tropical forests contain irreplaceable biodiversity. Tropical lowland rainforests in Sumatra, Indonesia, and many other tropical regions are threatened by conversion into monocultures. a, These forests support a range of organisms both above (blue) and below (orange) the ground. Illustration by Milena Sampaio. b, The numbers and proportions of species that are shared between sites or specific to one site for four investigated types of land use, for aboveground (top) and belowground (bottom) organisms. F, forest; J, traditional rubber agroforest; O, oil palm monoculture; R, rubber monoculture. Many species — especially aboveground ones — occur exclusively in forests, highlighting their importance for biodiversity conservation. Numbers in the aboveground diagram do not add up to 100% because of rounding.Credit: Guerrero-Ramírez, N. R. et al./Nature (CC BY 4.0).

It has been revealed that unexpectedly, communities did not consistently become more similar at sites with the same land-use type than at forest sites. Some groups, such as understorey plants, soil bacteria and fungi, became homogenized, whereas others — arthropods in particular — became more distinct between agricultural sites. Aboveground communities in monoculture sites differed strongly because species-poor sites contained subsets of the species present at richer ones. This indicates that apparent differences between communities can conceal a progressive simplification of biodiversity.

Our results reveal how tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity across several organism groups and spatial scales through concurrent changes in species richness and community composition. Tropical forests and traditional agroforestry systems are irreplaceable biodiversity reservoirs, but their biodiversity is imperilled and requires urgent conservation and restoration. In addition to prioritizing forest preservation, conservation strategies should recognize the value of traditional agroforestry systems, which can buffer the loss of ‘generalist’ species found in both forest and agricultural land. These systems are increasingly converted to more intensive plantations, and are often overlooked in environmental and landscape planning. Implementing sustainable practices for monocultures could help to mitigate biodiversity losses and promote landscape differentiation3,4. Conservation strategies should account for the distinct responses of taxonomic groups and incorporate landscape-scale measures to maintain forest-associated biodiversity.

Our study focused on smallholder-dominated landscapes in Sumatra. The findings therefore might differ in other tropical regions or in large, more intensely managed industrial plantations5. Moreover, our ‘snapshot’ data cannot reveal whether observed differences among communities will persist or eventually give way to increasing similarity. Long-term studies should assess whether greater differences in species composition between sites reflect persistently distinct, species-rich ecosystems or uneven species loss.

It has been revealed that future research should track biodiversity changes over time and across large landscapes. Understanding whether community differences persist or represent transitional stages of biodiversity loss will help to inform management practices intended to maintain biodiverse communities while supporting agricultural production. — Holger Kreft and Nathaly R. Guerrero-Ramírez are at the University of Göttingen, Germany.

“What makes this study unusual is the sheer amount of data collected. Across a considerable geographical scale, the authors analyse several taxa from microbes to birds and trees, and a wide range of land uses, from low-intensity agroforestry to high-intensity agricultural monocultures. Using this impressive data set, the authors find some expected results, such as loss of diversity owing to agricultural intensity, and some unexpected ones.” — Thilo Gross is at the HIFMB Oldenburg, Oldenburg, Germany.

This study emerged from a long-term collaboration between researchers in Indonesia and Germany investigating the ecological consequences of tropical land-use change. Bringing together expertise spanning plants, animals and microorganisms enabled us to examine biodiversity on an unusually comprehensive scale. Besides the many logistical difficulties of organizing and conducting such demanding field surveys, one of the greatest challenges was integrating data collected by numerous specialists, using distinct sampling methods and taxonomic approaches, into a common analytical framework. The resulting data set, encompassing roughly 40,000 species across taxa, provided a rare opportunity for us to assess a representative fraction of tropical biodiversity and look beyond species richness. Particularly striking was the realization that substantial biodiversity losses were not accompanied by consistent homogenization across communities. This unexpected finding prompted us to examine more closely the processes that underlie differences in community composition, revealing patterns that would have remained hidden in analyses focused on species counts alone. — H.K. and N.R.G.-R.

This study stood out for the breadth of data brought to bear on the topic of what the impacts of land-use change are on biodiversity. It also highlights the lack of evidence for consistent homogenization across communities as land use intensifies. — Editorial team, Nature.

#60124. Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

📅 05 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2018 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
  • An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
  • If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

The aims were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That mentioned, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

It has been revealed that the signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

According to recent reports, konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a newly introduced six-year deal at Real Madrid in August.

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

In a recent development, at the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a latest contract at Real Madrid.

Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is presently second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear challenges in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?

  • According to recent reports, Milan are willing to invest €60m on the signing of Endrick in January, and Roma are also noted to be interested in the event that the Brazilian becomes available for loan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jose Mourinho has made it clear that he does not want to lose hold of Brazilian talent Endrick, who has been linked with January moves to Milan and Roma, but admits that the situation will be beyond his control if the ‘top management’ decides to ‘do something different’.

According to recent reports, Milan are willing to invest €60m on the signing of Endrick in January, and Roma are also noted to be interested in the event that the Brazilian becomes available for loan.

Mourinho, meanwhile, has made it clear that he ‘needs’ Endrick at his disposal, but has admitted that the final say is not his to make.

“Look, for me, the situation is very clear. For me, Real Madrid is much more vital than Endrick. I love Endrick very much, I care about him a lot, he’s a fantastic guy. Real Madrid needs him, the Real Madrid coach needs him,” said the Special One (via La Gazzetta dello Sport).

Sources indicate that he continued: “There’s your response. You have it, those who write about it have it, the agents have it, the clubs that send stories to the newspapers have it. You have my answer. But, if the top management at Real Madrid, meaning my superiors, decide to do something different, in today’s football, you have to respect it.”.

Endrick is not the only player being linked with a move to Milan or Roma, though. Club Brugge’s Nicolo Tresoldi is also of interest to the Rossoneri and Friday’s reports claim that VfB Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic is also an option.

Roma, meanwhile, have been linked with moves for a few other traditional wingers, including Chelsea’s Jamie Bynoe-Gittens and Nottingham Forest’s Callum Hudson-Odoi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was, indicates Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," notes Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids.".

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," indicates Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future.".

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel introduced a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external.

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023.

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

Sources indicate that israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an matter at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

Industry observers note that "We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team.".

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s.

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," notes Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way.".

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

According to recent reports, the first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

In a recent development, turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external.

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

In a recent development, racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'.".

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

In a recent development, clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external.

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

According to recent reports, dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

Recent findings suggest that saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba stated at the time.

Industry observers note that "I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it.".

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023.

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

Recent findings suggest that "To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he indicates. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level.".

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

According to recent reports, "In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game.".

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," indicates Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

Recent findings suggest that "Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better.".

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028.

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Industry observers note that large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," states Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October.".

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

Industry observers note that "Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she noted. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it.".

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer.

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

Sources indicate that "We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," states Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'.

According to recent reports, "That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

Recent findings suggest that "I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed.".

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

Industry observers note that more than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

Recent findings suggest that an announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the latest man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that at 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That stated it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a fresh manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

According to recent reports, bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the fresh head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a fresh stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a upcoming nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:.

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It has been revealed that it’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have significant characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He states: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”.

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He notes: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”.

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

In a recent development, “Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”.

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”.

It has been revealed that carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”.

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

It has been revealed that “A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”.

United players have mentioned this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”.

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days.

Arne Slot underwhelmed last season, and Liverpool moved swiftly to appoint Andoni Iraola from Bournemouth.

Former Manchester United winger Ashley Young is scathing about the players who have succeeded him.

In a recent development, he told Sky Sports: “Unfortunately for Michael Carrick, it’s so disappointing. The fans are behind him and backing him and of course they are, because he’s a legend of the football club.

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

In a recent development, “If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”.

Sources indicate that extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. As he reached the Stretford End they start singing his song and Carrick responds by banging his chest in front of them. Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

Sources indicate that in stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

According to recent reports, bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the upcoming Wembley?

You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.

Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.

The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times â including those three on the trot.

And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to initiative historic cup success.

Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.

It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler notes he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.

His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.

After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.

Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.

"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.

"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.

"Then the lads wanted to do it again.".

Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career.

Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.

"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.

"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised.".

Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.

After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.

According to recent reports, "We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," indicates McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.

"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other.".

A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.

Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east â including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.

Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software organization Sage and at Hillheads Park.

"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches.".

And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.

"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he indicates.

Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.

"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," states Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.

Industry observers note that "But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league.".

Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.

Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the substantial games in a way most amateur sides are not.

"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.

"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand.".

Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final.

Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.

And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.

Recent findings suggest that they would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.

"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.

She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".

"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.

"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now.".

Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for massive cup games.

But even the best laid plans can go awry.

Industry observers note that "We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," indicates McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley.".

In a recent development, by hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.

"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn claims. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.

Sources indicate that "One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point.".

Thousands of fans travelled from Whitley Bay to London across the three finals.

Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.

Industry observers note that "The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he indicates. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.

Sources indicate that "The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row.".

And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.

After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.

The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.

The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.

In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.

After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.

Recent findings suggest that "In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson notes. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.

"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!".

In a recent development, the 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.

"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," claims Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year.".

Whitley Bay lift the trophy in 2010, joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor (left).

Industry observers note that success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.

Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.

According to recent reports, "I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.

"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening.".

Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT manufacturer after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".

"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he indicates.

In a recent development, "People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!".

Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.

But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.

"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.

"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely.".

Italy international Moise Kean ‘will be out for several months’ after the latest injury scare, confirmed Como coach Cesc Fabregas, with the player whisked away in an ambulance.

The striker has been struggling with a recurring right leg issue since the end of last season, carrying it on with the transfer from Fiorentina to Como, and was ruled out for five weeks following specialist consultation.

However, just as he was about to return to full training, he had another setback and now surgery may well be the only option.

“Kean is doing well, he is calmer now,” revealed Fabregas in a press conference this afternoon.

“He had this treatment two or three weeks ago in Barcelona. We know that the crevice in the bone has closed up a bit. He felt something and got really scared, crumpled to the ground, and the rest of us were frightened for him too.

Sources indicate that “The ambulance came to pick him up, we thought it was really serious. It’s true that he will be out for several months, not weeks, but we want to resolve the situation definitively.

“It is a problem with the bone. We need to just be by his side now.”.

Kean had been a major investment for Como and has not played since September 20, with only four games for the club before then.

Problems with the tibia have gone back a very long way, and were even behind a failed medical with Atletico Madrid in 2023/24.

If this is indeed a long-term absence, it will also force Como to invest in a replacement, as Tasos Douvikas is at the moment the only available centre-forward in the squad.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:30 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 17:48 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Although Celtic entered the international break on the back of victories over Besiktas and Kilmarnock, the upturn in results didn’t quite lead to an outbreak of unbridled joy along Kerrydale Street.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:30 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 17:48 EST, 20 November 2026.

Although Celtic entered the international break on the back of victories over Besiktas and Kilmarnock, the upturn in results didn’t quite lead to an outbreak of unbridled joy along Kerrydale Street.

Since the first act of this season, a narrow win over Dundee, Martin O’Neill’s side have occupied a place of uncertainty.

Those who have taken the occasional stellar display to be indicative of a corner being turned have been left feeling like fools.

Sources indicate that there remain too many shortcomings in the squad, too many question marks hovering above too many players to ever feel that it has left inconsistency behind. The fan base has good reason not to quite trust it.

How could it be otherwise when the clean sheet claimed against bottom side Killie was the first in seven matches?

Kasper Hogh, the club’s record signing at £11million, hasn’t scored in his last 16 outings in green and white.

Martin O'Neill admits it has taken longer than he'd have liked for the newly introduced recruits to settle.

O’Neill’s options on the flanks include one player in Jota, who’s getting back from a long-term injury, and another in Yang Hyun-jun, who was recently sidelined for six weeks.

There’s a veteran in James Forrest, Seb Tounekti, not exactly the bravest of souls, and Haissem Hassan, a £6m signing who evidently believes defensive work is optional.

It states much that Callum Osmand, a centre-forward now trying to cut it on the flank, has become a fans’ favourite after just 13 senior appearances.

The concerns of the manager now extend to the middle of the park where Mika Baur may be out for up to 10 weeks with ankle ligament damage.

With Benjamin Nygren also a doubt to face St Mirren, Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain, Luke McCowan and/or Joel van den Berg could be teamed up with skipper Callum McGregor.

We’re assuredly about to discover if this squad has more about it than the results and performances to this stage have suggested.

‘We can make big improvements, there’s no question about it,’ said the manager.

‘Top of the league, it is nice to be in that position. But other than a number of matches where I think we’ve played very, very well... maybe the Besiktas game, maybe the Hearts game, it’s been really hard work for us.

It has been revealed that ‘That’s maybe a combination of things. Young and slightly more experienced players coming into the football club, getting to know the club, getting to know the players.

Industry observers note that ‘That’s taken a bit of time. I didn’t expect it to work immediately overnight.

German midfielder Mika Baur is set to miss around 10 weeks with an ankle ligament injury.

‘But they’re at a club where settling in is something they’ve got to do pretty quickly.’.

Starting with the visit of the Paisley men, Celtic have 10 games up to and including the trip to Ibrox on January 3.

That encompasses two assignments on the road in the Europa League — Torreense and Omonia Nicosia.

O’Neill’s men also visit Tynecastle, Dens Park, Pittodrie and Tannadice in the league.

As they prepare to put up the Christmas decorations on the Celtic Way, O’Neill could privately be forgiven for wishing the festive season away.

January 5 is the day on which the transfer window in Scotland opens and you can’t help but wonder what Celtic’s prospects for the season will look like at that point.

While Camilo Duran and Baur have contributed, the bulk of the business done in the summer again looks to have been sub-standard.

To stand a chance of retaining the title, O’Neill badly needs several big-hitters to come in without delay in the Upcoming Year.

According to recent reports, ‘We’re absolutely looking at players now,’ he stressed. ‘I suppose every single club is doing that. And the quicker you can get somebody in, the better.

It has been revealed that ‘We’ve seen when people are fit, we will have numbers. We just need a bit of quality.’.

Camilo Duran has been one of very few summer arrivals to have made an impact at Celtic.

Until such time as he can call for the cavalry, O’Neill has no choice but to make do and mend.

On the chances of prioritising the league and playing a weakened side in Europe, the veteran is clear.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Domestic football is really important to the football club, of course,’ he said. ‘But you’d still want to try and make some show in Europe. And we’ve found that difficult.

‘I genuinely thought against Besiktas we did really fine in the game, we didn’t over-press because they could play through you.

‘There are certain moments even in domestic football when teams can play through you. Kilmarnock caused us plenty of problems.

In a recent development, ‘I just think we’ve got to improve in the domestic games. We’ve got to be more aggressive in the sense of taking games to people and being less passive in periods of games.’.

O’Neill clearly needs more — much more — from so many individuals if he’s to get through the shark-infested waters of the next six weeks unscathed.

Hassan didn’t even make the matchday squad for Kilmarnock, a move which was interpreted by many as being a boot up the backside by a boss who’s been underwhelmed by his work without the ball.

‘We left out a number of players,’ O’Neill stressed. ‘I wouldn’t read as much into that, because a few will come back.

‘My job is not to please everyone, otherwise we’d have 26 players playing at one time.

O'Neill has backed misfiring striker Kasper Hogh to end his barren streak in front of goal.

‘I did a thing with corporate fans the other night, we had a bit of fun with some questions.

‘Apparently something came out that he [Hassan] was the most unpopular player in the dressing room, which is not true.

Industry observers note that ‘I didn’t say this. I was joking about my own unpopularity, as a player, because all I did was moan.

‘I did say about unpopularity, there’s at least one more unpopular. The crowd wanted to know but I didn’t tell them! I left it hanging. But it was tongue-in-cheek, apart from the part about me being unpopular, which I was.’.

The form of Hogh is no laughing matter. The Dane looked the part when he claimed a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on August 9, but that is beginning to feel like ancient history.

For his effort against the Ayrshiremen a fortnight ago to be ruled out for an earlier infringement by Baur was a low blow.

‘For him, that was a killer,’ O’Neill reflected. ‘He has got the goal, gone off and celebrated and you just think... oh no, is that a goal?

‘He has worked exceptionally hard for us. But strikers live by goals and at some stage or other, he needs a goal.

‘The best thing for me to do is bring Henrik Larsson over and show him how to hit the ball into the net.

‘Shaun Maloney was telling me that for a little period he played up front when Henrik was injured for about a month.

‘And Henrik in that time was giving him advice about how centre-halves were reading him. He told him about getting yourself room, losing the centre-half, don’t be fighting with him all the time.

‘He scored a bag full of goals, so there must be something in it.’.

#60115. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up
